In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of ethylene in wood formation.
the movement and possible metabolism of gaseous ethylene in dormant Norway spruce (Picea abies) stems.
the possible role of ethylene in wood formation in conifers, and the movement of ethylene and its possible metabolites in trees.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no movement or metabolism of ethylene or ethene in the stem of Picea abie.
the movement of ethylene and possibly ethane is restricted to the apoplasm of the wood and that the ethane produced in the wood is metabolised by ethane oxidase.
there are two different pools of ethylene, one that is metabolically active and one that is not.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ethylene concentration in dormant P. abies is very low and the movement of applied ethylene is upwards.
the endogenous concentrations of C 2 H 4 are low, but that C 2 H4 is produced and metabolized in the stem of Picea abie s.
ethylene is not involved in the regulation of bud dormancy in P. abies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ethylene concentration is kept very low in dormant Piceas, and that ethylene applied in a stem is transported upwards.
the movement of ethylene and possibly ethane can be detected and that ethane can be used as a tracer of the movement of ethane.
it seems to be important to maintain a low ethylene concentration in the wood-forming tissues of Picea abie.
